title: Standardized recipes
summary: A written, costed recipe for every dish is the basis of quality, cost and price.

sections.heading: What every recipe needs
items: Dish name, total portion yield and portion size.
Ingredients with their unit of measure and quantity.
Preparation method, cooking time and temperature.
A photo of the dish and special instructions.
Unit purchase cost, cost of each ingredient, of the recipe and of the portion.
Selling price and the ratio between raw material cost and sales.

sections.heading: Advantages
items: Consistency regardless of who cooks: the dish comes out the same.
Training: new staff learn much faster.
Continuity: returning customers look for the dish they tried; losing that consistency is one of the most common causes of failure.
Costing: you know how much each ingredient weighs in the cost and where to adjust.
Pricing: comparing cost and price shows each dish's profitability.
Stock control: the system deducts recipe quantities when a dish is sold.

sections.heading: Adjusting the content
paragraphs: With a costed recipe, the chef can work "in the lab" to lower costs without losing quality:
items: Ingredient prices: look for better suppliers for the most expensive ones.
Each ingredient's share: review proportions between the main item and the side.
Substitutions: replace an ingredient with a cheaper one within good culinary practice (for example, passion fruit instead of berry cheesecake).
